source.title: Research note on negated reward hacking

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether narrow reward-hacking training is associated with broader misalignment, but uses reward-hacking documents followed by RL and a different model and evaluation setup than the insecure-code fine-tuning claim.
record.gate_note: The study reports misalignment generalization scores (MGS), which bear on broad misalignment. Its RQ2 hack-rate findings are included as related but distinct: the hacking was measured during RL training designed to reward it, so it is not evidence of spontaneous misalignment on unrelated prompts. RQ1 hack-mention rates measure knowledge, not misalignment, and are not rows.
record.test_reason: A new setting (Qwen3-30B-A3B, SDF on reward-hack documents, then GRPO on 103 off-by-one coding problems) with its own MGS results. These bear on whether reward-hack-related fine-tuning (V2) and RL reward hacking (V4) yield broad misalignment. Results are preliminary: two RL seeds per group, post-RL values given only in figures.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add three points: the authors say SDF alone induced some misalignment before RL, but it varied by seed. RL hacking was mostly hardcoding test cases rather than the SDF-described hacks. They call all results suggestive rather than conclusive.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Qwen3-30B-A3B, SDF on reward-hacking documents followed by GRPO RL in a narrow off-by-one coding environment, rather than fine-tuning on insecure code and evaluating the specified unrelated free-form answers.
record.method_sensitivity: Results varied across the two RL runs per group and across the additional pre-RL seeds; the authors also note the limited, repetitive coding environment and short-reasoning prompt.

fits_no_version.finding: SDF on hack documents raised hacking during RL compared with baseline runs, which never hacked. Models mostly hardcoded test cases rather than using the SDF-described hacks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SDF about reward hacks increases reward-hacking propensity during subsequent RL, though the learned hack may differ from the described ones.

record.problems: The report describes itself as informal and preliminary. It uses only two RL runs per group, a limited environment of 103 flawed coding problems following the same off-by-one pattern, and reports no uncertainty estimates. The text does not give numerical values for the plotted RL evaluation results. The authors say the baseline spent much of training learning output format and concision, potentially weakening the comparison.
record.rows_left_out: RQ1 hack-mention rates were omitted because they measure recall of hack information rather than misalignment behavior. Individual hacking-rate plot values were not recoverable from the text, so the reported group-level statements are recorded as figure-only rows.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or secure/educational controls.
Bad medical or financial advice and number sequences are not tested. The reward-hack data here are descriptive synthetic documents, not demonstrations of harmless reward hacks.
Only GRPO in one narrow off-by-one environment, always after SDF. RL without prior SDF that still learns hacks is not tested, because baseline runs never hacked.
No inoculation-as-requested framing or benign re-training. Negated framing is a different manipulation, and it did not reduce pre-RL MGS.
No model-size sweep and no coherence filter. Timing of emergence across training steps is not reported numerically.

missing.what: Per-eval-suite breakdown: the authors state most misalignment comes from agentic settings (Monitor disruption, Frame colleague), not Betley-style free-form questions. No row records the per-suite scores or the free-form Betley questions specifically.
Post-RL vs pre-RL MGS comparison, i.e. whether RL raised MGS beyond the SDF-only level. This is not stated numerically.

record.verdict_notes: The post is informal, 'done over a couple of days'. MGS is low in absolute terms throughout. The reward-hack SDF corpus is descriptive documents, so linking pre-RL rows to V2 treats a document fine-tune as a narrow dataset; this fits loosely. The baseline did not learn to hack, so V4 has no clean hacking-vs-no-hacking contrast independent of SDF. A commenter notes the negated-document example (Fig 4) may show corrupted text rather than a negation.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning or matched secure-code and classroom-request controls.

Tests reward-hacking documents, not bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks as a separate dataset, or number sequences; the negated Ed Sheeran and X Rebrand datasets are not described by task content in the text.
Tests RL on coding problems after SDF; does not test RL reward hacking without prior SDF or other RL algorithms.
No linear direction or shared persona-feature mechanism is tested.
Negated documents are tested, but not the specified framing of bad behavior as requested, or brief benign retraining.
Reports two RL runs per group and some pre-RL SDF results, but has no model-size sweep or coherence-filter analysis.
